            Maura Derrane on 30 years in television and the importance of believing in yourself

            RSVP had such a fun day catching up with Maura at the gorgeous Intercontinental Hotel, where we chatted about health, careers and what is really important in life

            Comments0
            News
            Jane Lundon Editor of RSVP Magazine and RSVP Live
            17:53, 07 Oct 2026Updated 18:05, 07 Oct 2026
            Listen to audio version of this article
            Sponsored by
            0:00 / 3:46
            Instaread

            RTE presenter Maura Derrane may be 30 years on our screens this year but she has no intention of slowing down. Starting in the newsroom with TG4 and finding her way to afternoon TV in RTE, the Galway girl has resonated with audiences from day one. With a passion for fashion, wellness, lifestyle and current affairs - presenting the Today Show is the ideal gig for our favourite Gaeilgeoir.

            ‌

            “I'm actually 30 years on air now consistently without a break, which is amazing, really, when you think about it.” Maura told RSVP, continuing she said, “I was very lucky that I fell into the career that was to be my whole life and broadcasting will do that, you know, media, broadcasting, journalism. I started as a journalist, then became a presenter, so it's kind of full circle, but I think that it's such a brilliant area because it's so vast.

            ‌

            “You can never get bored in an area like this because there's so much involved in it, you can constantly divert to different disciplines. And now there's online, there's podcasts, there's all sorts, there's a whole realm of media that is there now for the next generation and forward generations, which is great.”

            ‌

            Pneumonic plague risks explained - symptoms, treatment and how to prevent

            Celia Holman Lee experiences 'major health setback' and is receiving medical care

            Maura agreed her chosen career is a precarious one but advises that you cannot get into the industry if you are worried about the next step. Explaining, she said: “It's only in this last year that I've been made staff at RTE, before that I was a contractor. So I worked year to year, not knowing if I had a job every September. And yes, that is very precarious, but it takes a certain mindset to be able to live within that realm. And I'm lucky that I never worried too much about the next year. I always felt, even if one door closed, even if the show I was working on finished, I figured that another door would open.”

            Speak about confidence and her self belief, Maura said: “I don't think I was brought up to have confidence. My mother was very good at instilling, do what you like best, not what you think you should do.

            ‌

            "If you're unhappy in something, don't continue to be unhappy in that field.

            "She never told us you need to go to school, you need to work really hard, you need to pass all your exams, go to college. It was never that It was always what makes you happy and find out what makes you happy. I really do believe there is a career, job and a place in life for everyone but it shouldn’t be all about career either, that is the difference with the young people today, they have more balance.”
